units.text: Start in the left panel. IP-based routing uses CIDR collections and location mappings for known client networks. The information visible through the querying resolver affects how those ranges are matched.
Move to the upper right. Geoproximity uses the locations of users and resources. Bias expands or shrinks a resource's geographic catchment instead of specifying a client network range.
Read the lower-right panel. Supported geoproximity records can be configured directly. Traffic Flow is useful when the routing logic needs a more complex, reusable decision tree.
With the full slide visible, choose the actual input: client network, geography or measured latency. Test unmatched locations and resolver behavior before relying on the chosen routing policy.
Read the left panel. Public endpoint checks evaluate configured HTTP or HTTPS responses, or TCP connection behavior. Use the intended hostname and path, and allow the checker traffic.

Follow the child results in the upper-right diagram. A calculated health check combines other checks using configured thresholds. That aggregation is separate from the health checkers' own endpoint observations.
Move to the lower-right example. Public checkers cannot directly reach a private address. A supported metric-based alarm signal provides one way to monitor private application readiness.
Review the original slide. These are selected health-check designs, not every available option. Measure the failure you intend to handle, test missing data, and prepare the failover destination.

Follow the diagram on the left. A versioned Traffic Flow policy defines routing logic. A policy instance applies that logic to create DNS records; the definition and resulting records are different resources.

Inspect the upper-right panel. Geographic bias changes catchment size, while weights influence DNS answers. Resolver and client caching prevent either from guaranteeing an exact share of individual application requests.
Read the lower-right checklist. Review record scope, TTL, health behavior, costs and fallback cases before rollout. Test both authoritative answers and the behavior observed by clients.
With the full slide visible, retain the previous policy version and plan rollback. A changed policy and a refreshed client answer are separate events, so validate the cached client path.
